intro: The Hebrew Bible is the oldest collection of texts in this course and one of the most influential books in the world. Jews read it as the Tanakh, their scripture. Christians read it as the Old Testament, the first part of their Bible. Muslims honor many of its figures, among them Abraham, Moses, David and Elijah, as prophets. Its stories, laws and poems have shaped courtrooms, protest movements, music and everyday English, from a still small voice to a time for everything.

This unit reads the Hebrew Bible in the order Jews arrange it. Chapter 27 stays in the Torah: creation, the covenant with Abraham, the Exodus and the laws of Sinai, with a Passover Seder in Skokie as the doorway. Chapter 28 moves through the Prophets and the Writings: kings and prophets, the fall of Jerusalem and the exile in Babylon, and the psalms, wisdom books and short stories that are still read and sung in synagogues and churches.

By the end you will be able to name the three parts of the Tanakh and place key books in them, explain covenant and prophecy in the Hebrew Bible's own terms, cite a verse by book, chapter and verse, and describe fairly how Jewish and Christian readers read the same passage in different ways. As in every unit, the goal is to understand how communities read their texts, not to decide what anyone should believe.
bigQuestion: How has one ancient library of law, story, prophecy and poetry been read so differently, and so faithfully, by the communities that hold it sacred?

test.q: What are the three parts of the Tanakh, in order?
test.why: The Tanakh's name comes from its three parts in order: Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).

test.q: What is the sign of God's covenant with Noah?
test.why: Genesis 9 sets the rainbow as the sign of the covenant with every living creature; circumcision is Abraham's sign.

test.q: What does the Passover Seder do with the story of the Exodus?
choices: Reads it silently in the synagogue
Acts it out only for children
Retells it at a meal so each person sees themselves as if they had left Egypt
test.why: The Haggadah guides the Seder and asks every participant to see the Exodus as their own experience.

test.q: How does rabbinic Jewish tradition read the story of Eden, compared with Augustine?
choices: As a first choice between two inclinations, not inherited original sin
As a story about the Sabbath
As a prophecy of the exile
test.why: Augustine taught original sin; rabbinic teaching reads Eden as the first exercise of human choice.

test.q: Why do lists of the Ten Commandments differ between traditions?
choices: Each comes from a different original language
They divide and number the same text differently
test.why: Jews, Catholics and most Protestants share the text of Exodus 20 but count its commands in different ways.

test.q: Which command does Leviticus 19 ground in the memory of Egypt?
test.why: Leviticus 19:34 commands love for the stranger, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

test.q: Which prophet confronted King Ahab and met God in a still small voice?
test.why: 1 Kings 18 and 19 tell of Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel and the still small voice at Horeb.

test.q: What did Amos say God wanted instead of festivals from people who crushed the poor?
test.why: Amos 5:24 asks that justice run down as waters and righteousness as a mighty stream.

choices: Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple
test.why: Nebuchadnezzar's army destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple in 586 BCE; Assyria took the north in 722 BCE.

test.q: Which foreign ruler does Isaiah 45 call the LORD's anointed?
test.why: Isaiah 45 calls Cyrus of Persia the LORD's anointed because he allowed the exiles to return.

test.q: The Hebrew word mashiach, anointed one, is the root of which English word?
test.why: Messiah comes from mashiach, one anointed with oil, as Samuel anointed Saul and David.

test.q: Which book is read aloud on Purim?
test.why: Purim celebrates the story of Esther, which is read aloud from a scroll; Ruth belongs to Shavuot.

test.q: Isaiah 7:14 reads virgin in the King James Version and young woman in the 1917 JPS translation. What does this show?
choices: One of the translations is a printing error
The Hebrew text of Isaiah was lost
Christians and Jews read different books of Isaiah
test.why: The KJV follows the Septuagint and Matthew; the JPS follows the Hebrew almah. Each choice reflects a reading.

test.q: How do Proverbs and Ecclesiastes differ in outlook?
choices: Proverbs is poetry; Ecclesiastes is law
Proverbs is about kings; Ecclesiastes is about priests
Proverbs says wise living usually goes well; Ecclesiastes asks whether anything lasts
They share the same outlook word for word
test.why: Proverbs teaches that wisdom usually pays; Ecclesiastes calls everything hevel, vapor, and questions lasting gain.

test.q: Which is a neutral scholarly name for the text Jews call the Tanakh and Christians call the Old Testament?
test.why: Hebrew Bible names the shared text without taking either community's side.

write.prompt: What does a people owe the stranger, the poor or the exile? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Leviticus 19:34, Amos 5:24, Jeremiah 29:7 or Ruth 1:16, and explain how Jewish and Christian readers understand each one and why.
tips: Name each text by book, chapter and verse, and say which translation you quote.
Attribute every belief to its tradition: in Jewish tradition, many Christians hold.
Explain the context of each passage: who is speaking, to whom, and when.
Compare the readings rather than judging which one is right.
Use the unit's terms, such as covenant, prophet, exile and diaspora.
